correctness.rationale: Each increasing r-tuple specifies exactly one r-edge shortcut witness; E W_{n,r}=binom(n,r)(c/n)^r. A length-r undirected cycle has a witness under exactly 2r of the r! relative vertex orders. Factorial moments of short cycle counts give independent Poisson means c^r/r!, overlap of distinct bounded-length cycles is O(1/n), and expected longer witness counts are bounded by sum_{r>L} c^r/r!. Consequently all witnesses are disjoint with high probability and coincide one-for-one with transitive-redundant arcs; the marked and total Poisson limits, matching property and expectation follow. The finite checker executed from the candidate package and passed 67,738 tests; it is not the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Specific random-order transitive-reduction and marked-Poisson statement was compared against accessible original random graph orders, dependent-arc theory, directed-acyclic null models and transitive-reduction literature. None of the inspected results gives the present simple-Bernoulli c/n count and certificate-length spectrum. Disjoint cycle-Poisson counts are acknowledged classical; what is distinct is the orientation thinning plus identification with the unique reduction. Inaccessible full text and general-cycle literature remain explicit priority risks.
residual_risks: Rödl–Thoma (2005) is highly relevant but only its abstract was accessible; its complete contents were not examined.
A general theorem on sparse acyclic orientations or Poisson cycle functionals could imply the stated specialization even if it uses different terminology.
Prior-claim search was evidence of non-overlap among accessible records, not proof of worldwide uniqueness.

value.rationale: Transitive reduction is a canonical minimal reachability representation of a causal or precedence DAG. In the c/n independent-edge null model, the count of removable relations is a natural operational invariant, not a contrived statistic. The independent certificate-length spectrum c^r/r!, explicit e^c-1-c-c^2/2 deletion law, and high-probability vertex-disjoint unique proofs explain not only how many edges are redundant but the complete finite mechanism by which they arise. This yields interpretable exact asymptotic benchmarks for sparse ordered networks, and is not the generic undirected-cycle count alone.
